New talk on the open model economy. I wanted to break down the case of where open model builders should steer the economics of the industry, if we want to avoid being swallowed by OpenAI and Anthropic in due time. This rests fully on being able to drive the cost of inference down dramatically on specialized, repetitive tasks, rather than trying to compete on cost with the frontier labs in any general agent.

A core piece of it is how the open model economy is very fragmented, leaving an interesting puzzle we need to solve to get revenue from applications to feed back into the next model cycle. This is a very near-term problem as closed labs scale rapidly.

This talk investigates:
Are people using open models?
How close are open models to the frontier?
Mapping the open model economy
How open models win

This is a practice recording of my talk "How Open Models Win" for Fireworks Forge 2026 in San Francisco (3 November 2026), which will have improvements over this one.

article.plain_text:
TL;DR: H200 loses money even when fully busy. B300 makes money once it's 35% busy. Which GPU card you rent matters more than which inference engine you run.
A common claim on X and LinkedIn is that inference is an easy business: demand is so high that anyone who can rent GPUs can sell tokens at a profit, with no technology of their own. This post checks that claim against public data.
Two views of the same market
Let's be fair about the technology first. Open-source inference engines are mature now. vLLM and SGLang are production-grade, and DeepSeek just open-sourced DeepInfer, the engine behind its own API (DeepInfer deployment Q&A). The vLLM team reproduced DeepInfer's decode throughput within 6% on the same hardware (vLLM, Oct 23, 2026). And even so, I know several companies that hand-wrote their own engines and got excellent results. Friends at inference providers confirm it: a hand-rolled engine can reach that level too. So the engine is a solved problem, whichever way you get one.
Then there's the other camp: it's a price war, margins are 10% at best and often negative. They point to OpenRouter, where 29 providers sell the same DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and the cheapest lists input at $0.056 per million against ~$0.30 for most, below cost by any math (Jeff Xiong, Oct 23, 2026; OpenRouter provider listing). OpenRouter's own data says the quiet part: V4's token volume roughly doubled in the first half of 2026 while its share of spend barely moved (OpenRouter Insights, Jul 2026).
Both sides cite real numbers. The "DeepSeek makes $38 a GPU-hour" camp (DeepInfer deployment Q&A, Oct 2026) and the "everyone on OpenRouter is losing money" camp are measuring different things.
 
 
Source: List and off-peak prices: DeepSeek API pricing; realized blended input and cache-hit prices: OpenRouter V4.1 Flash 1017 provider page, 2026-10-26
So in this post I use only public data: GPU rental prices, measured throughput of one model on each card, the precision each card can actually run, and what the market actually pays per token. One model, one traffic pattern, one speed promise, one price, one rent. Only the card changes. The question is simple: if you buy or rent cards and host a model, do you make money?
The short answer
Yes, it can be profitable, but only on Blackwell, only if your cards are busy more than a third of the time, and only if you don't race to the bottom on price. An 8×B300 node at 50–70% utilization runs a 31–51% gross margin. H200 does not break even at any utilization.
Methodology
The setup below is held fixed throughout. Changing any part of it changes the answer, so it is worth stating precisely.
Model: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It's the #1 open-weight model on OpenRouter by a wide margin, roughly 30% of all tokens in the week of Oct 19–25 (OpenRouter rankings), and it's the only model with public third-party measurements on all three cards.
Traffic: SemiAnalysis's AgentX workload: 393 real Claude Code sessions replayed, median input 142k tokens, median output 444 tokens, ~95% of input is cache hits (AgentX methodology). This is what OpenRouter traffic actually looks like in 2026: the top 10 apps are all coding agents (OpenRouter apps), and agentic traffic is 7x human traffic with ~87% of tokens served from cache (OpenRouter, "Cache is Crucial", Oct 8, 2026). Chatbots are a small share now.
Speed promise: 100 output tokens/s per user. The median OpenRouter provider does ~35 (SemiAnalysis, InferenceX v2), so this is strict, but it's the one level where all three cards have numbers.
Throughput: best public open-source engine result on InferenceX for each card (H200, B300, GB300 NVL72), vLLM / SGLang / Dynamo, FP4 weights everywhere. H200 runs FP4 weights through dequant kernels; Blackwell runs native FP4.
Price: what OpenRouter providers actually collect on this model today: $0.013 per million input tokens (blended across cached and uncached) and $0.57 per million output (OpenRouter, V4.1 Flash 1017 providers). With a 99/1 input/output mix that's $0.019 per million total tokens. Not list price. Not DeepSeek's off-peak price. What the market pays.
Rent: lowest publicly visible on-demand price. H200 $3.99, B300 $7.40 (Hyperstack). GB300 NVL72 has no public rack price, so I used the SAVRN index at $15.21 (SAVRN GPU price index).
Utilization: tokens you actually sold ÷ tokens the benchmark says you could sell. Not GPU busy time. A new provider with no direct customers, relying on OpenRouter routing alone, lands at 10–30%. DeepInfra puts typical self-hosted inference at 10–20% (DeepInfra, Aug 2026), which matches what new providers have told us.
One formula: gross margin per GPU-hour = tokens/s × 3600 × price × utilization − rent. No bandwidth, no people, no spare capacity. If it doesn't work here, it won't work with those added.
H200 vs B300 vs GB300 NVL72: which GPU is profitable for inference?
At the price the market pays today, H200 cannot cover its rent, an 8×B300 node breaks even at 35% utilization, and a GB300 NVL72 rack breaks even at anywhere from 24% to 84% depending on how it is configured.
Throughput and rent on their own don't compare across cards. Divide one by the other and you get the number that does: how much rent you burn per million tokens at full load. The market pays $0.0188 per million, so that's the line to beat.
 
 
Source: Computed from the table above; market price = OpenRouter realized price for V4.1 Flash 1017, 2026-10-26
The last column summarizes the article in a single number. The percentage in brackets is also the break-even utilization: if rent eats 35% of the price at full load, you need to be 35% busy to cover it.
Then what each card earns. Dollars per GPU are not comparable across cards that cost 2–4x different rents, so the fair yardstick is gross margin: 1 − rent ÷ revenue. I use 50% as the bar: below that, bandwidth, people, spare capacity and the occasional idle week eat what's left.
 
In dollars, for the two that work: a B300 clears about $2,400 per GPU per month at 50% busy and $5,500 at 70%; a rack-tuned GB300 clears $12,500 and $22,000.
 
Source: Computed from the two tables above: gross margin = 1 − rent ÷ (full-load revenue × utilization)
 
Source: Throughput: InferenceX AgentX runs and vLLM blog (Oct 2026); price: OpenRouter realized price for V4.1 Flash 1017; rent: Hyperstack on-demand, SAVRN GB300 index, 2026-10-26
Three results stand out.
H200 can't cover its own rent at 100% utilization. Full load earns $1.6/hour against $3.99 rent. This is not a pricing problem or a tuning problem. Hopper has no FP4 compute units, so a model built around FP4 runs at 1/13 the throughput of a B300 while costing half as much. Software doesn't fix a 13x gap.
B300 is the practical starting point. An 8-GPU node breaks even at 35% and is clearly profitable above 50%. Note that 35% is already above where most new providers land, so this only works if you bring 1–2 direct customers with you. OpenRouter routing alone won't get you there.
GB300 NVL72 is the best and the worst option, depending on who tuned it. Same rack, same model: the standard InferenceX config needs 84% utilization to break even; the vLLM team's rack-level setup with prefill/decode disaggregation and Wide-EP needs 24% (vLLM, Oct 23, 2026). A 3.5x spread from configuration alone. If you can't reproduce that tuning, you're better off with B300s.
What utilization do you need to break even?
An 8×B300 node needs 35% utilization, a GB300 NVL72 rack needs 24–84% depending on tuning, and H200 would need more than 100%. A new provider relying on OpenRouter routing alone typically reaches 10–30%.
 
Source: Throughput: SemiAnalysis InferenceX AgentX runs and vLLM blog (Oct 2026); price: OpenRouter realized provider price for V4.1 Flash 1017; rent: Hyperstack on-demand, SAVRN GB300 index, 2026-10-26
Look at where the grey band sits. That's where you'll be in month one. Only one bar lives there, and it's the one that requires a full rack and an engineering team that can reproduce a vLLM blog post.
 
Source: Computed from the table above: margin = full-load revenue × utilization − rent, × 730 hours
The slope is the card's earning power; the intercept is the rent. H200 is a flat line below zero. B300 is the only line that is both cheap enough to start and steep enough to matter.
Why do estimates of inference margins differ so widely?
Estimates of this business differ widely because the hardware ranking never changes (H200 < B300 ≈ GB300), but three business variables swing the break-even for the same B300 node from 20% to 93%:
 
 
Source: Computed from the sensitivity table above; B300 throughput from InferenceX AgentX, 100 tok/s base case
How did GPU rental prices change in 2026?
Of the three variables, rent is the one you control least, and in 2026 it went the wrong way. GPUs are supposed to depreciate. This year every generation got more expensive to rent, including the A100 from 2020: H200 on-demand rent is up 163% since January, B200 up 122%, H100 up 36% (a16z, Charts of the Week, Oct 23, 2026, using Ornn's Compute Price Index). Every one of them now rents above a six-year straight-line depreciation curve, the H200 by 143%.
 
Source: Year-to-date index and depreciation premium: Ornn Compute Price Index as charted by a16z (Oct 23, 2026); Oct 25 prices: data.ornn.com
The timing tells you why. H100 and B200 rents fell to about 77% of their January level in February and March, then snapped back in April, the same month agentic token volume on OpenRouter started its vertical climb (OpenRouter rankings). Rent follows token demand with a lag of weeks, and token prices follow competition with no lag at all. That is the squeeze: your cost went up 2x while your price went down, and both moves were set by other people.
Two practical consequences. First, the rents in this post are the cheap end of the market, not the middle: Ornn's executed-transaction index on Oct 25 has H200 at $6.30 and B200 at $9.70 per GPU-hour against the $3.99 and $7.40 Hyperstack list prices I used (data.ornn.com). At index rents, the B300 break-even moves from 35% toward 50%. Second, a 3–6 month reserved contract signed now is a bet that token demand keeps outrunning Blackwell supply. In 2026 that bet has paid; it is still a bet.
Take all three "good" and a B300 breaks even at 10%. Take all three "bad" and it loses money at 100%. The most optimistic estimates assume the good column; the most pessimistic assume the bad column. Each is correct for its own assumptions.
What inference provider pricing pages don't show
If these margins look thinner than what some providers appear to earn, it is because successful providers rarely sell exactly what the listing describes. The following practices are worth knowing before comparing prices on OpenRouter.
The model name is the same. The weights are not. Everyone lists "DeepSeek V4.1 Flash" or "GLM 5.3", but the cheapest endpoints run 4-bit weights, the expensive ones run 8-bit. On GLM-5.2, DeepInfra, Nebius and Parasail serve FP4, Novita and SiliconFlow serve FP8 (Artificial Analysis, GLM-5.2 providers), and NVIDIA quotes DeepInfra's cost per million tokens dropping from 20¢ on Hopper to 5¢ on NVFP4 (NVIDIA, Feb 2026). That 4x is where the "30% below list" prices come from. OpenRouter shows the precision only in a small tag on the endpoint, and about 95% of endpoints don't declare one at all. Baseten does it in the open: on GLM 5.3 their FP4 endpoint sells at list price and their FP8 endpoint is the "Fast" tier at 1.5x (OpenRouter, GLM 5.3). Same model, two products.
Quantization is not free, but it's not the main way quality gets cut either. On paper FP4 is nearly lossless now: NVIDIA's NVFP4 build of V4.1 Flash moves every benchmark by less than 1.5 points against DeepSeek's own checkpoint (GPQA Diamond 91.3 vs 91.0, Terminal-Bench 2.1 82.2 vs 81.6; NVIDIA release, Sep 16, 2026). Real users notice anyway: one team quantized GLM-5.2 to NVFP4, saw identical benchmark scores, and rolled it back after coding customers reported the chain of thought collapsing (umans.ai, Jul 2026). But the bigger cuts are cheaper than quantization. When Artificial Analysis scored the same models across providers in August, the most restrictive GLM-5.2 endpoints scored half the reference on scientific reasoning because of output-token caps, some gpt-oss-120b endpoints scored 22% on tool calling against 37% for the reference, and the worst endpoints produced roughly half the reference's reasoning tokens (Artificial Analysis, Endpoint Accuracy Index, Aug 4, 2026). Every one of those cuts raises tokens per second, which raises revenue per GPU-hour, which is why they happen. The labs have started policing it: Moonshot open-sourced a Kimi Vendor Verifier in April (GIGAZINE, Apr 21, 2026), and on Kimi K3 the providers that submitted now sit within about 4 points of the official API (Kimi-Vendor-Verifier results). The ones that don't submit are the ones to worry about.
 
Source: Moonshot AI, Kimi-Vendor-Verifier results for Kimi K3, DeepSWE column (github.com/MoonshotAI/Kimi-Vendor-Verifier), read 2026-10-26
Cache pricing is a routing weapon, not just a discount. OpenRouter pins a session to the same provider for 10 minutes only if that provider's cache-read price is below its input price (OpenRouter, sticky routing). So a low cache price buys you the follow-up requests, which are the cheap ones to serve. Providers who don't understand this get every request re-routed by price and watch their own cache hit rate collapse. The flip side: if you promise a cache discount but your KV memory can't hold the sessions, you pay full prefill cost on tokens you billed at 2%.
Price is the ranking algorithm. OpenRouter's default routing weights providers by the inverse square of price, so a provider at $1 gets roughly 9x the traffic of one at $3 (OpenRouter, provider routing). New providers also sit in an "insufficient data" tier until they've served 100 general and 200 tool-call requests, and Auto Exacto re-scores every endpoint every five minutes on tool-call success and throughput (OpenRouter, Auto Exacto). Free endpoints are the extreme version: MiniMax M3.1 Flash (free) and Nemotron 3 Ultra (free) are in the top 10 by tokens while their paid versions are a rounding error (OpenRouter rankings). That's subsidized traffic to buy ranking and data, not demand.
The benchmark counts tokens you don't get paid for. AgentX throughput is "total tokens" including cache hits. DeepSeek's 155 trillion tokens a day and $38 per GPU-hour are at off-peak prices with roughly 96% of input cached (DeepInfer deployment Q&A). Do the division and the real price is about 1 cent per million tokens. Anyone who quotes "25,000 tokens/s × $0.60" is using the output price, which applies to only 1% of the tokens.
The token business is often not the business. Look at what the incumbents actually sell: Together's and Fireworks' pricing pages lead with dedicated endpoints and GPU clusters by the hour, and Fireworks' on-demand H100 went from $4 to $8 an hour in a year (Fireworks pricing; Together pricing). The cheap per-token API is what brings customers in. The money is made on dedicated endpoints, priority tiers at 1.25–1.5x, region surcharges (Fireworks charges 1.5x for US-only), batch discounts at 50% and paid cache retention (DeepInfra, Aug 2026). If your plan is "list on OpenRouter and sell tokens", you are competing on the one product the big providers use as advertising.
The same practices, summarized. The right-hand column is how you catch it as a buyer, or what you'd have to decide as a seller.
 
Two common misconceptions about inference economics
Cached tokens are cheap to buy, not free to serve. 95% of the tokens flowing through your box are cache hits billed at $0.003–0.006 per million. They still occupy HBM and still trigger partial recompute. DeepSeek's $38/GPU-hour number comes from a 128+ GPU disaggregated deployment with ~100 PiB of SSD holding agent sessions for three days (DeepInfer deployment Q&A). That is not something 8 GPUs replicate.
You can't fill a rack from OpenRouter alone. A GB300 NVL72 at 70% utilization has to sell ~1.5 trillion tokens a day. That's 20–40% of everything OpenRouter routes to this model (~4–7 trillion a day, per OpenRouter rankings). You will not get that from OpenRouter's routing. An 8×B300 node needs ~1% of it, which is roughly what a mid-tier provider actually gets. What limits you is how many tokens you can sell, not how many you can produce.
 
Source: OpenRouter weekly rankings (Oct 19–25, 2026: ~51.6T tokens/week for V4.1 Flash) and a 30-day read of ~124T; rack and node volumes computed from InferenceX AgentX throughput at 100 tok/s per user
And as I said last week: this is increasingly an SEO business. OpenRouter allocates traffic on price, latency and uptime (OpenRouter provider routing), so everyone optimizes for the algorithm. Which means the price column above drifts toward "bad" over time unless you have customers who pay you directly.
So, is it profitable?
The engine is not the problem. vLLM is within 6% of DeepSeek's own DeepInfer on the same hardware (vLLM, Oct 23, 2026). The open-source stack is done.
The problem is everything around it: the card (Blackwell or nothing), the configuration (a 3.5x spread on the same rack), the price you can actually hold, and the traffic you can actually attract. Small teams can make money on 8×B300 at 50%+ utilization with a couple of direct customers. They will not make money racing to the floor on OpenRouter, and they will not make money on H200 no matter what they do.
The three numbers that decide profitability
Beyond the benchmarks, profitability comes down to three numbers nobody can look up for you:
Your throughput, not SemiAnalysis's. Replay a real agent trace on the exact checkpoint you'll serve, at 50 and 100 tok/s per user. First attempts land at 50–70% of the published number.
Your rent, not the list price. Get a signed quote. For GB300 it has to be a full NVL72 rack with the NVLink fabric, or it's a different machine with the same name.
Your price, not the model's. One week of real customers tells you what you actually collect per million tokens, how much of it is cache, and how many tokens a day you can really sell.
Put those three numbers into the formula above and you have your own answer. This post only shows you what the answer depends on.
So here's my answer to the question in the title.
The engine is free. The model is free. The benchmarks are public. Anyone can get all three, which is why 30+ providers are selling the same model at 30+ different prices. None of them has an advantage the others can't copy next week.
What isn't free: Blackwell at a reasonable rent, an engineer who can reproduce a vLLM blog post, and customers who pay you directly instead of through a ranking algorithm. Have all three, and an 8×B300 node pays for itself at 35% utilization and is solidly profitable above 50%. With only two of the three, you are effectively subsidizing your customers' workloads.
Hosting an open-source inference engine produces tokens, not profit. Getting paid for those tokens is a separate business, and most providers on OpenRouter are not really in it.

Earlier last week I posted my calculation that went viral that projected so much compute coming online next year per SemiAnalysis power availability data, that we would need 2.5T revenue to consume all that, even assuming only 50% of compute for inference at - wait for it - DeepSeek V4.1 Flash rates.

I have been running the numbers again and again and have realised the numbers are even more insane than I initially calculated on basis of SemiAnalysis power addition projection, and DS Flash inference economics validated by vLLM and SGLang teams!!!
There is too much compute coming online. However, proponents of Jevon's paradox have a great track record. This is sincere attempt to see both side of the arguments by modeling the scenarios. Please do review and let me know what you think.
What changes?
* SemiAnalysis 50 GW power number for 2027 was net new addition and not cumulative power. So that much power will be available by end of 2027.
* So cumulative power from 2025 - which is mostly for AI - is 91.6 GW by end of 2027 (Astra has the same interpretation after seeing the article. SemiAnalysis team, please correct me if I got it wrong).
 
Source Article: https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/datacenters-2027-the-year-of-acceleration
Assuming there are enough accelerators to consume all that capacity (there are per SemiAnalysis at least in 2027), total revenue projection at revenue rate of 100B / GW for 2027 are insane at 4.5T USD. And remember we are assuming DS Flash prices in this analysis which with their architecture and efficiency offers 100B USD revenue per GW even assuming lot of slack.
See the chart to see projections for 2025, 2026 and 2027. From 2025 to 2027 we are assuming inference increasing from 10% to 50% overall compute and revenue per GW rising from 20B/GW to 100B/GW.
 
Does it mean we would have a massive glut? 
Not necessarily.

1. Lot of supply could be consumed for demand that can not be measured in token revenue (e.g. Google search, Meta Muse)
2. There might be massive collapse in token prices reducing per GW revenue from 100B / GW to something like 20B / GW (with that overall token dollar value goes from 4.5T to approximately 1T USD. In that case the global economy 'may' be able to absorb the supply, otherwise not.). But this model is based on 20% of DS Flash pricing!!! Compared to OpenAI and Anthropic pricing, this is ridiculously low already. To reach those levels the leading US labs may have to cut prices by 20 times.
3. Models may become so cheap, we may use large models for everything (why use Haiku class models when you can use Fable Opus/Opus for everything).
4. Most models may get served at high interactivity at low batch sizes. Why not everyone gets 'FAST', if there is capacity!
5. This may enable new application (real time voice assistant that are every expensive at 3$ per hr,  digital companions, personalised entertainment, robotics etc. Global education industry will completely get transformed). However, existing labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are not yet interested in this space, certainly not beyond robotics and use of their models in education. This is a massive opportunity for the startups in the space.
6. 'Continuously on' cyber security may consume a decent amount capacity as well (not only design time reviews, but theorem proving, run time security etc.)
However, there are too many variable that need to fall in place for this capacity to be absorbed so rapidly - there are only 15 month, and so it is not guaranteed. Probability of it not happening (absorption) is far higher that it getting absorbed.
What about training costs?
Also, we are assuming 50% of total capacity that is 45.9GW (capacity costing 459 B a year at 10B/GW) for training. Recall Anthropic till date since its foundation has spend just under 16B USD on model training & research (interpretability). 16B was enough to get you from Claude 2 all the way to current generation with all the model lineages: Mythos, Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku. I find it hard to believe that for major labs put together - Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, MSL and xAI -  training expense to run 459B ARR by end of the next year end. I suspect most of the compute would have to be absorbed by free services like Google Search and Meta Muse.
What if prices and demand adjust the compute supply & Jevon's paradox plays out by end of 2027?
While this low probability scenario, it is still likely. If token prices and demand adjust to consume available capacity we would see following:
LLM Model prices with respect to intelligence would be down by around  20 times (this would be in line with the trend predicted by EpochAI). I am assuming tough competition between leading labs eroding pricing power, as it is hard to form oligopoly when there are 5 players in the market, and it is also illegal.
Model lab profit margins will have collapsed from 70-90% to below 30-20%. Not bad because volume would be enormous - approximately 1 T USD ARR by 2027 end. They will be roughly making  20B USD/GW and paying 10B USD/GW to hyperscalars.  They will cut down on training costs and inference may be more than 50% of compute use (we assumed 50% in this article for 2027, if you recall). Saving on training costs is the only way to hit 30-20% profit margins with such low rates. 
Remaining compute after LLM labs squeeze of training would be used by Search, Muse and personal experience (companions, entertainment) & Robotics. I expect golden age of AI powered startups that are model builders as well.
Labs will negotiate hard with hyperscalars to cut down per GW cost to below 10B USD/GW. Hyperscalars will negotiate hard, in turn, to cut prices for semiconductors. Hyperscalars have advantage of scale and custom silicon program, so this may be disadvantage Neo-Clouds (at least long tail ones).
Efficient use of electricity and efficient chips would be paramount from hyper-scalar perspective at they try to reduce compute rental cost. We will see advantage for vendors offering that. We will see further emphasis on ASIC programs to cut rental of 1GW of compute to below 10B USD/GW by avoiding Nvidia tax. We will see lot of interest in both: Mature silicon that offers high amount tokens / MW (advantage Nvidia) as well as new approaches that avoid Nvidia tax and reduce power demand (OpenAI Jalapeno)
Global AI revenue (ex-China, as SemiAnalysis numbers are ex-China) would be approximately 1T USD per year by end of 2027 in this modal, requiring 147 USD revenue from every living human (on average). Hard but not impossible given average GDP per capita ex-China is 14,518$. So this is 1% of that, and people spend more than that amount on telephone services.
 
However, the real issue is capacity does not stop coming online in 2027, it keeps on getting added in 2028, 2029, 2030 and so on; and chips last really long. All the valuations are built on this assumption that 1T USD buildout and spend will continue in perpetuity. Hence, I am calling out AI overbuilding and requesting you to think how hard it is to consume all the capacity.

I may be wrong and will change my opinion, if I see a better argument. But I am afraid we are into full blown overbuilding phase.

It is so frustrating and short-sighted that we haven’t updated export controls to stop this. This loophole has been reported for years. Commerce controls high bandwidth memory chips in 3A090.c. But unlike for AI chips, it does not have a corresponding control in 4A090 that also controls items that CONTAIN a high-bandwidth memory chip. This is why a high-bandwidth memory chip in isolation is controlled, but a chip soldered to a board is not. This makes no sense. 

The fix here is easy: add a new control to 4A090.c that reads, “c. Computers, "electronic assemblies," and "components" containing integrated circuits, any of which meets or exceeds the limits in 3A090.c.” That’s it, problem solved. All shipments of items that contain high-bandwidth memory chips would require a license.  

Also, if Commerce actually takes that advice, at the same time it should also update the regs so that 3A090.a and 4A090.a also include the memory bandwidth and interconnect parameters that Commerce has privately subjected Nvidia, AMD, and others to since April 2025, but has never made public. Putting these requirements into public regulations and making them applicable to every company could have helped stop some of this smuggling. It’s also very basic good governance, as export controls should wherever possible be transparent and applied uniformly, not private and applied only on certain companies. 

This is yet another consequence of Commerce not taking export controls seriously. The next time BIS claims they are doing more on export control enforcement than ever, remember this story, the Megaspeed fiasco, and the many others like them that are published every week. Export control enforcement has never been worse.

An announcement that is as personal as professional:

18 months ago, we started collecting online prices in real time to track how Liberation Day tariffs were feeding into inflation.

A lot has happened since. The BLS commissioner was fired. The longest government shutdown in US history meant CPI wasn’t published for the first time. And the case for an independent measure of inflation became much stronger.

What started as a tariff inflation tracker has since grown into something much bigger: 

The Bloomberg Price Project (BPP), our attempt to build the US CPI from the ground up using alternative data.

Today, BPP covers 87% of the CPI basket, across both goods and services (more new data will be added in coming weeks). Every month, we collect millions of prices from card transactions, e-commerce sites, grocery stores, pharmacies, rental listings, corporate data, Bloomberg Terminal market prices and government records. And more data are coming.

The payoff is detail. Official CPI data let you drill down to categories such as “uncooked beef steaks.” BPP goes much deeper — breaking the CPI basket into almost 700 line items, compared with roughly 200 in the official data.

Brought to you by: myself, Troy Durie, Daniel Ripperger-Suhler, Joshua Danial and Scott Johnson from across Bloomberg Economics.
